body: {"total":19,"records":[{"title":"Pharmacist-led follow-up for patients starting oral anticancer agents: a randomised trial of adherence and unplanned admissions","authors":"Moreno-Achterberg L, Osei-Whitfield K, Tanaka-Brandt R","year":2019,"venue":"Oncology Pharmacy Research","doi":"10.5555/opr.2019.0271","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We randomly allocated 212 adults starting capecitabine or a tyrosine kinase inhibitor to pharmacist-led follow-up, with a consultation before the first cycle and telephone checks at days 7, 14 and 28, or to usual oncology follow-up. At 12 weeks, adherence by pill count was 91 percent with pharmacist follow-up and 79 percent with usual care. Unplanned admissions within 90 days occurred in 9 percent and 15 percent respectively, a difference compatible with chance. Relative dose intensity was 0.87 and 0.92. The trial was not powered for admissions or toxicity."},{"title":"Costs and savings of an oral chemotherapy pharmacy clinic: a single-centre budget analysis","authors":"Fairweather-Obi D, Lindqvist-Ramos P","year":2022,"venue":"Cancer Services Economics","providerType":"report","abstract":"We estimated the annual cost of a pharmacist-led oral chemotherapy clinic for 400 patients and the admissions it might avert. The clinic cost about 118,000 a year in pharmacist time and overheads. Using admission rates before and after the clinic started and an average cost of 7,400 per toxicity admission, averted admissions were valued at between 64,000 and 141,000 a year depending on assumptions. The before-after admission rates were not adjusted for case mix, and costs to patients were not included. The authors present the result as a budget range, not a net saving."},{"title":"Measuring adherence to oral anticancer agents: agreement between pill counts, pharmacy refill data and electronic caps","authors":"Gunasekara-Holm T, Adeyemi-Fischer B","year":2017,"venue":"Cancer Adherence Methods","doi":"10.5555/cam.2017.0045","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In 96 patients taking oral anticancer agents, we compared three adherence measures over 12 weeks. Mean adherence was 93 percent by pharmacy refill data, 88 percent by pill count and 81 percent by electronic caps. Refill data overestimated adherence compared with electronic caps by 8 to 12 percentage points, largely because patients who collected supplies on time did not always take doses as scheduled. Self-report was highest of all at 97 percent. The authors recommend that studies state which measure they use and avoid comparing results across measures."},{"title":"Telephone toxicity checks by oncology pharmacists and dose intensity of capecitabine","authors":"Vasquez-Nnadi C, Holloway-Sato J","year":2021,"venue":"Oncology Pharmacy Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared 164 patients receiving capecitabine with pharmacist telephone toxicity checks against 171 patients treated before the checks were introduced. Grade 3 or worse diarrhoea or hand-foot syndrome fell from 21 to 13 percent. Dose reductions were made earlier and more often with the checks, and relative dose intensity over the first three cycles was 0.86 against 0.91. Survival was not assessed. The authors note that earlier dose reductions may trade toxicity for dose intensity and that the balance needs longer follow-up."},{"title":"Patients' views of pharmacist support when taking cancer treatment at home","authors":"Kiplagat-Bruun E, Castellanos-Hart M","year":2020,"venue":"Patient-Centred Cancer Nursing","doi":"10.5555/pccn.2020.0133","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We talked with 26 patients taking oral anticancer agents at home about pharmacist telephone follow-up. Patients valued having a named person to call about side effects, and several said they would otherwise have waited until the next clinic visit to report problems. Some found repeated calls intrusive once they felt confident. Patients living alone and those with limited English described the most difficulty managing complex schedules, but they were under-represented in the study. The authors suggest tailoring the frequency of calls to each patient."},{"title":"Interventions to support adherence to oral anticancer agents: a review of 31 studies","authors":"Oyelaran-Petersen H, McAllister-Iwu S, Brennan-Dube A","year":2023,"venue":"Oncology Care Reviews","doi":"10.5555/ocr.2023.0510","providerType":"review","abstract":"We identified 31 studies of interventions to support adherence to oral anticancer agents, including 12 randomised trials. Pharmacist-led interventions were the most common. Effects on adherence were inconsistent, partly because adherence was measured in at least six different ways, and effects were largest when measured by self-report. Only 7 studies reported unplanned admissions and 4 reported costs. Few studies included patients over 75 or patients who did not speak the local language. The authors call for standard adherence measures and reporting of harms."},{"title":"Unplanned admissions within 90 days of starting oral anticancer therapy in a regional cancer network","authors":"Delacroix-Mwangi F, Stroud-Nakamura P","year":2016,"venue":"Cancer Services Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across five cancer centres, we followed 3,120 patients starting oral anticancer agents. Eighteen percent had an unplanned admission within 90 days, and 49 percent of these admissions were attributed to treatment toxicity, most often diarrhoea, neutropenic fever or hand-foot syndrome. Risk was higher in patients over 75, patients living alone and those living more than 100 kilometres from the centre. The authors suggest that early follow-up should prioritise these groups and that services should be designed for patients who cannot easily travel."},{"title":"Pharmacist time per patient in oral chemotherapy follow-up programmes: a multi-centre time study","authors":"Andersson-Okafor G, Whitlock-Rao N","year":2024,"venue":"Oncology Pharmacy Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We timed pharmacist activities in oral chemotherapy follow-up programmes at four cancer centres over eight weeks. Pharmacist time per patient over the first 12 weeks of treatment was a median of 2.6 hours, ranging from 1.4 to 4.1 hours between centres, with most time spent on the first consultation and on toxicity calls. Centres that used structured call scripts spent less time per call. The authors estimate that one full-time pharmacist can follow about 450 new patients a year alongside other duties."}]}
